summary: Short vision paper naming 'context rot' — AI configuration files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions, .cursorrules) going stale as code evolves — and proposing a roadmap that reuses documentation-consistency tools. As preliminary evidence, the unmodified DOCER README checker is run on 612 config files from 356 randomly sampled repositories, flagging stale code-element references in 23.0% of repos.

claims.claim: Stale code-element references occur in 23.0% of repositories (95% CI 18.8-27.2%).
claims.evidence: Table 1: 82/356 repos, 230 stale of 18,048 verified references (1.27%). But manual check of 50 flagged elements found only 32 (64%) genuine (Table 3, single annotator); the 23.0% repo-level figure is not adjusted for the 36% non-genuine rate, and median stale refs per affected repo is 1, so the true repo rate is likely lower.

claims.claim: Traditional documentation-consistency tooling can already surface context rot without modification.
claims.evidence: DOCER applied unchanged (§3.2); 64% precision on 50-sample; two-snapshot design misses references introduced after first commit (acknowledged).
Asserted in §1 and posed as open RQ3; no behavioral measurement in this paper.

patterns.note: Repo instruction files are widely used but ~1.3% of verified references go stale and some repos accumulate rot; impact on agents untested.
Deterministic regex + git grep two-snapshot check detects referential rot cheaply; recommends deterministic detection with LLM repair.
Proposes consistency checks for config files as a CI-style linter; not built here.
Lists MCP tool-description drift as an open transfer opportunity.

methodology.sample: 356 of 4,420 eligible repos (random seed 42) from Galster et al. dataset; 612 config files; 29,454 candidates; 18,048 verified.
methodology.variance: 95% CI on repo proportion; no precision CI.
methodology.languages: Not broken down by programming language.

standards.artifacts: Online appendix with analysis script, per-element results, repo versions, DOCER regexes, 230 stale references, 50 annotations; input dataset on Zenodo.

biases.detail: Headline repo-level rate counts tool flags with only 64% precision; and staleness is not shown to affect agent behavior.
Precision estimated from 50 elements by one annotator, no inter-rater agreement.

coi.detail: Second author is also an author of the input dataset (Baltes et al. Zenodo), not a COI.

verdict_reason: Transparent, reproducible, random-sample feasibility study that is directly relevant to maintaining AGENTS.md-style files; but the headline 23% is unadjusted for 36% false/ambiguous flags, precision rests on one annotator and 50 items, and the paper does not show that rot harms agents.
applicability: Directly actionable for a team with several repositories and mixed hosts: each repo will carry AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/copilot-instructions variants, and references to Java classes, packages, and scripts will drift. A cheap deterministic CI check (extract identifiers/paths from instruction files, verify they exist at HEAD) is justified as hygiene; generating host-specific files from one committed source reduces divergence across hosts. Do not budget for it as a correctness lever until impact is shown — the corpus has a controlled ablation suggesting context files themselves do not move correctness much.

conflicts_with.detail: Context rot is motivated by the assumption that stale context files degrade agents; the two-agent ablation found context-file strategy did not measurably change correctness, which would bound the harm of rot.
